screens.title: Setting Up Your First Hyperledger Fabric Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will set up a reliable Hyperledger Fabric development environment so you can run a local sandbox network and deploy sample chaincode. We will focus on the concrete tools you need — Docker and Docker Compose to host Fabric components as containers, a supported runtime for chaincode such as Go or Node. js, and classic utilities like curl and Git. You will see how to download the official fabric-samples and Fabric binaries using the provided install script, add the binaries to your PATH for convenience, and use the test-network scripts to bring up, use, and tear down a two-organization sandbox. Along the way I’ll show common pitfalls: Docker not running, permission issues, port conflicts, and environment variables that must be set when you invoke peer commands. By the end you’ll be able to run the network, create a channel, deploy the asset-transfer-basic chaincode, perform a read and a write operation, and then cleanly shut the network down. This foundation matters because a correct local environment saves hours of debugging and ensures reproducible hands-on experiments. Ready to begin with the prerequisites and the download step?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Setting Up Your First Fabric Environment
Getting ready to run test-network
Install prerequisites, fetch fabric-samples, and learn the lifecycle commands you will use throughout this chapter.
In this lesson
Install and verify Docker, language runtimes, download samples, run network.sh to create a channel and deploy chaincode, then perform query and invoke operations.
Concept map
Prerequisites
Docker, Go/Node, curl, Git
Download
fabric-samples & binaries
Test Network
up, createChannel, deployCC, tear down
Why this matters

A stable local environment is the fastest path to experiment with Fabric, iterate on chaincode, and troubleshoot network behaviors without affecting a shared staging system.

Sample terminal steps
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperledger/fabric/main/scripts/install-fabric.sh | bash -s -- -l 2.5.8 -d -b
export PATH=$PATH:$PWD/fabric-samples/bin
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh up
./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel
./network.sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp ../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go
./network.sh down

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to set up, run, and manage a local Hyperledger Fabric test network and perform basic chaincode interactions. First, you will identify and install required software: Docker and Docker Compose to run Fabric components as containers, a chaincode runtime such as Go or Node. js, plus curl and Git for downloads and repository management. Second, you will download the fabric-samples and Fabric binaries using the official install script, understand the directory layout created, and add the binaries directory to your PATH so the Fabric CLI tools are available anywhere. Third, you will bring up the provided test-network using the network. sh script, create a channel, and deploy a sample chaincode. Finally, you will invoke read and write operations against the chaincode and safely tear down the network. Each of these skills removes a common blocker when starting Fabric development and ensures your experiments are repeatable. We will also practice verifying installations and common quick checks that prevent the most frequent errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on the hands-on commands and environment hygiene that keep your Fabric experiments repeatable. You will practice adding the fabric-samples bin directory to your PATH so commands like peer and orderer are immediately available from your shell. You will also learn to set key environment variables used by the peer CLI to target an organization and peer, such as CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, which let you run queries and invoke transactions as a specific admin. Another objective is clean teardown: using network. sh down and, when necessary, Docker cleanup commands so stray containers and images do not cause port conflicts. Finally, you will follow best practices for version compatibility and verification so Docker images, Fabric binaries, and chaincode runtimes match. These skills prevent many common errors and speed up development iterations when building and testing chaincode.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
01 — Add Fabric binaries to PATH

Make the binaries directory available in your shell session and persist it in .bashrc or .zshrc so peer and orderer commands are call-ready without typing full paths.

export PATH=$PATH:$PWD/fabric-samples/bin
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
02 — Set peer environment variables

Target a specific peer and organization for CLI commands by setting CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, and related variables.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
03 — Clean teardown & Docker hygiene

Use ./network.sh down after experiments and prune Docker when necessary. Understand that docker system prune -a removes all images and is a last resort.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
04 — Verify versions & compatibility

Confirm Docker, Docker Compose, Go or Node.js versions, and that Fabric binaries and Docker images are matched. The install script helps align these components.

screens.title: Prerequisites: What and why
screens.narratorSegment: A correct prerequisites set is the simplest, most effective risk reducer when working with Hyperledger Fabric. The core idea is straightforward: Fabric runs its components — peers, orderers, CAs, and chaincode packaging — inside Docker containers. That makes Docker and Docker Compose essential. If Docker is not running, network startup will fail immediately. For chaincode you need a supported runtime: Go or Node. js are common choices in examples; choose the runtime you intend to develop in and install the correct major version. Curl and Git are utility tools: curl fetches the install script and binaries, while Git clones the fabric-samples repository for examples and scripts. A concrete example: if Docker Desktop is stopped, running./network. sh up will produce container creation errors. A common misconception is that Fabric tools alone are sufficient — they are not; without Docker the Fabric binaries cannot start peers or orderers. Another common trap is mismatched versions: Docker engine and Compose must meet minimums, and chaincode runtime versions must match your development examples. Takeaway: verify docker --version and docker compose version, confirm go version or node -v, and ensure curl and git respond. This verification step saves multiple hours of debugging downstream.

keyIdea.title: Install and verify
keyIdea.text: Verify Docker, a chaincode runtime, curl, and Git before attempting to run the test-network to avoid avoidable failures.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Prerequisites: What and why
Required tools and verification
Run these commands to confirm installations and versions.
docker --version
docker compose version
go version   # if using Go chaincode
node -v      # if using Node.js chaincode
curl --version
git --version
Why Docker matters: Fabric uses containers to isolate peers, orderers, and chaincode runtimes.
Why a runtime matters: chaincode executes in a language runtime that must be compatible with your examples.
Why curl/git: they fetch install scripts and the fabric-samples repository for example code and scripts.
Concrete example
If docker --version shows no daemon, ./network.sh up will attempt to create containers and fail. Start Docker Desktop or the Docker daemon and retry.
Common mistake
Running network.sh without Docker running or with mismatched Docker Compose leads to container creation and networking errors that are often misdiagnosed as Fabric bugs.
Key Takeaway

Confirm and match versions for Docker, Compose, and your chosen chaincode runtime before proceeding. This simple step avoids the majority of early failures.

screens.title: Downloading Fabric samples and binaries
screens.narratorSegment: Downloading the fabric-samples and the matching Fabric binaries is a single scripted operation that both fetches tools and aligns versions. The canonical command provided uses curl to download and run the install script with specific flags to choose a Fabric release and request Docker images and binaries. In practice you run the curl command exactly as given to create a fabric-samples directory and populate a bin folder with tools such as peer, orderer, and configtxgen. After the script completes, it is good practice to add the bin path to your shell PATH so you can run Fabric commands from any directory. A concrete example: run the curl command with the specified version label to download release 2.5.8 and include -d and -b to fetch images and binaries. A common misconception is that manually pulling Docker images is necessary; the install script handles images if invoked with the download flag. Step-by-step: run the curl line, inspect fabric-samples/bin, then export PATH=$PATH:$PWD/fabric-samples/bin and persist that line in. bashrc or. zshrc. Confirm by running peer version. This process ensures the CLI tools you need are available and version-consistent.

keyIdea.text: Use the install script to fetch the right binaries and images, then add fabric-samples/bin to PATH for immediate CLI access.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Downloading Fabric samples and binaries
Run the install script
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperledger/fabric/main/scripts/install-fabric.sh | bash -s -- -l 2.5.8 -d -b
This command downloads the script and requests Fabric binaries and Docker images for the specified version. The script creates a fabric-samples directory and places binaries under fabric-samples/bin.
Add binaries to PATH
export PATH=$PATH:$PWD/fabric-samples/bin
Persist this line in your profile so peer and orderer commands are always accessible. Verify with peer version.
Common misconception
Some learners try to manually copy binaries into system folders. Let the install script manage downloads and use PATH to reference them; manual placement can cause permission and version confusion.

screens.title: Bringing up the test-network
screens.narratorSegment: Bringing up the test-network is the first full end-to-end run you will perform. The network. sh script in fabric-samples/test-network orchestrates Docker container creation for two organizations, each with a peer, and a Raft ordering service. To begin, cd into fabric-samples/test-network and run./network. sh up. The script pulls or reuses Docker images, starts containers, and prepares cryptographic materials and configuration required for the network. You will see log output from containers as they initialize; this output is useful for diagnosing startup issues such as missing images or TLS certificate problems. After up completes, create a channel and deploy chaincode using the separate network. sh commands. A practical example: after./network. sh up completes, run./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel to create a channel and then./network. sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go to deploy the Go chaincode. Common mistake: running up while Docker is not started or when ports like 7051 and 7050 are already occupied by other services. Always verify Docker is running and ports are free. The network up command gives you a reproducible local Fabric environment for development and testing.

keyIdea.title: Orchestrated local network
keyIdea.text: Use ./network.sh up to provision a repeatable two-org Fabric sandbox that you can use to test channel and chaincode operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Bringing up the test-network
Start the network
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh up
This command starts two org peers and a Raft ordering service inside Docker containers and prepares the crypto materials used by the network.
Next steps after up
./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel
./network.sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp ../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go
Create the channel and deploy chaincode to see the full create-invoke-query workflow against a channel shared by Org1 and Org2.
Key Takeaway

./network.sh up provides a fast, repeatable sandbox. Ensure Docker is running and ports are available before invoking it.

screens.title: Creating a channel and deploying chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Once the network is up, the next concrete steps are creating a channel and deploying chaincode. Channels create a private ledger between organizations; in the test-network you will create mychannel to be shared by Org1 and Org2. Use./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel to create the channel and generate the necessary configuration. After the channel exists, deploy sample chaincode with./network. sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go. This deploy command packages the chaincode, installs it on peers, and commits it to the channel. A concrete example: when you run deployCC for the basic chaincode, the script compiles the Go chaincode, installs the package on both peers, approves the definition, and commits it to the channel. A frequent misunderstanding is to expect chaincode files already to be active after up; creating a channel and deploying chaincode are separate steps. Another pitfall is specifying an incorrect chaincode path or language; match -ccp and -ccl to the chaincode you intend to deploy. After deployment, you can set peer environment variables and run peer chaincode query and invoke commands to interact with ledger state. The channel and deployment sequence is the core flow for enabling application-level interactions with Fabric.

keyIdea.title: Enable ledger interactions
keyIdea.text: Create a channel and deploy chaincode so peers share a ledger and can process transactions and queries.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Creating a channel and deploying chaincode
Create the channel
./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel
This command sets up the channel configuration and has Org1 and Org2 join the channel so they share the ledger.
Deploy the sample chaincode
./network.sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp ../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go
This packages, installs, approves, and commits the chaincode so it becomes available on the channel for query and invoke operations.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm ./network.sh up completed without errors before creating a channel.
  • Ensure -ccp path and -ccl language match the chaincode you deploy.
  • After deploy, set peer variables and test queries and invokes.

screens.title: Setting peer environment variables
screens.narratorSegment: To interact with deployed chaincode you must instruct the peer CLI which organization and peer to act as. Fabric uses environment variables for this purpose. Important variables include CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, which names the MSP for the organization; CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, which points to the admin identity that will sign transactions; CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE, which references the TLS certificate for the peer; and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, which gives the host and port for the target peer. A concrete example for Org1 is to set CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID to Org1MSP and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS to localhost:7051, and to set CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH to the admin msp path provided in fabric-samples/test-network organizations structure. Once these variables are set in your shell, peer chaincode query and peer chaincode invoke commands will act under that identity. A common misconception is that the peer CLI auto-detects the intended organization; it does not. You must explicitly set these variables or source the scripts the test-network provides. Closing question: can you identify which environment variable controls the identity used for signing transactions? Answer: CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH. This explicit configuration model keeps CLI operations precise and auditable. Setting peer environment variables means set core_peer_* variables so the peer cli sends requests as a specific org admin to the correct peer endpoint.. In practical terms, configure the cli to operate as a specific organization and peer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Targeted CLI context
keyIdea.text: Set CORE_PEER_* variables so the peer CLI sends requests as a specific org admin to the correct peer endpoint.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Setting peer environment variables
Example Org1 admin environment
export PATH=${PWD}/../bin:$PATH
export FABRIC_CFG_PATH=${PWD}/../config/
export CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED=true
export CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID="Org1MSP"
export CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt
export CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/users/Admin@org1.example.com/msp
export CORE_PEER_ADDRESS=localhost:7051
These values point your peer CLI at Org1’s admin identity and peer0 so you can query and invoke chaincode as that organization.
Checklist & misconception
  • Ensure CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH points to an admin identity used to sign transactions.
  • CORE_PEER_ADDRESS must match the peer’s Docker port mapping.
  • CLI commands will fail if CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE is incorrect when TLS is enabled.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly set peer environment variables so your CLI actions execute in the intended organizational context.

screens.title: Querying and invoking the sample chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Interacting with deployed chaincode demonstrates a complete read-write cycle on the ledger. Once you’ve set peer environment variables for Org1, run a query to see current world state using peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'. This example returns an empty array initially. To create an asset, invoke the CreateAsset function with peer chaincode invoke and provide the function and arguments in JSON form, including the orderer address and TLS options. The invocation triggers transaction flow: endorsement by peers, ordering, and committing to the ledger. A concrete example is invoking CreateAsset with arguments for asset id, color, size, owner, and value. After invoking, query GetAllAssets again to verify the asset appears. A common misconception is treating invoke and query interchangeably; invoke performs state-changing transactions and requires an endorsement and orderer interaction, while query is read-only and does not generate a ledger transaction. Always ensure your peer environment variables are set and that you include correct TLS options and peer addresses when invoking across organizations. This read-then-write-then-read pattern is essential to validate chaincode behavior during development. Querying and invoking the sample chaincode means use query for reads and invoke for writes. verify results by querying after an invoke to confirm ledger updates.. In practical terms, use peer chaincode query and peer chaincode invoke to read and write ledger state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Querying and invoking the sample chaincode
Query all assets (read-only)
peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'
This returns current world state for assets visible to the channel, for example an empty array if none exist.
Invoke CreateAsset (state-changing)
peer chaincode invoke -o localhost:7050 --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls --cafile ${PWD}/organizations/ordererOrganizations/example.com/orderers/orderer.example.com/msp/tlscacerts/tlsca.example.com-cert.pem -C mychannel -n basic --peerAddresses localhost:7051 --tlsRootCertFiles ${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt --peerAddresses localhost:9051 --tlsRootCertFiles ${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org2.example.com/peers/peer0.org2.example.com/tls/ca.crt -c '{"function":"CreateAsset","Args":["asset1","blue","5","Tom","1000"]}'
Tip & misconception
Tip: Query after an invoke to confirm ledger changes. Misconception: invoke is not a query; it creates a transaction that must be ordered and committed and may require multiple peer addresses and TLS certs for multi-org endorsement.

screens.title: Tearing down the network
screens.narratorSegment: A clean teardown is as important as a correct startup. Use./network. sh down to stop containers and remove generated artifacts for the test-network. This command revokes running processes and removes temporary crypto materials and Docker containers created by the up command. Routine teardown prevents resource leakage, port conflicts, and accidental interactions between successive runs. If the environment becomes inconsistent—stale containers, orphaned images, or dangling volumes—you can use docker ps -a to inspect containers and docker stop followed by docker rm to remove them. A last-resort measure is docker system prune -a to remove all containers and images, but be mindful this deletes everything and can be disruptive. A common mistake is leaving containers or networks running which later cause port collisions on ports such as 7050 or 7051. Another pitfall is assuming down always fixes everything; sometimes manually removing volumes or images is necessary. Takeaway: always run./network. sh down at the end of a lab, verify with docker ps -a that nothing Fabric-related is running, and reserve system prune for cases where normal cleanup fails. Tearing down the network means use ./network.sh down after experiments and remove stray containers to prevent conflicts in subsequent runs.. In practical terms, clean up containers, artifacts, and avoid dirty environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting a Fabric development environment is often about checking predictable causes. This screen gives a comparison of issues, likely causes, and remedies. First, 'Docker not running' manifests as container creation errors when running./network. sh up; remedy: start Docker Desktop or the Docker daemon and verify docker --version. Second, 'Permissions and sudo' may cause commands interacting with Docker to fail if your user is not in the docker group; remedy: either run with sudo where required or add your user to the docker group and re-login. Third, 'Port conflicts' show up when another service is bound to ports like 7050 or 7051; remedy: stop conflicting services or remove conflicting containers with docker ps -a and docker stop. Fourth, 'Incorrect environment variables' cause peer CLI commands to fail or target the wrong peer; remedy: re-export the CORE_PEER_* variables or source the test-network environment script. A common misconception is to assume Fabric itself is failing; often the root cause is Docker, permissions, ports, or PATH misconfiguration. When deeper issues persist, check container logs, re-run network. sh down, and consider pruning Docker images as a final corrective measure. The fastest path to resolution is to methodically validate each likely cause in this checklist.

Issue: Docker not running
Symptom: network.sh up fails with container creation errors.
Remedy: start Docker daemon / Docker Desktop and rerun docker --version to confirm.
Issue: Permissions
Symptom: Docker commands require sudo or fail for your user.
Remedy: add your user to the docker group or use sudo where necessary, then relogin.
Issue: Port conflicts
Symptom: Containers fail to bind to expected ports like 7051 or 7050.

screens.title: What the test-network provides
screens.narratorSegment: The test-network is a compact representation of a full Fabric deployment, useful for development and learning. It provides two organizations, each with a peer that maintains ledger state and endorses transactions, and a Raft ordering service which orders transactions into blocks for commit. The network also generates cryptographic materials for MSPs and TLS so you can test secure communications. The key benefit is that you can exercise the full transaction lifecycle—endorsement, ordering, and commit—locally without deploying to a multi-host production environment. A concrete example: when you invoke chaincode requiring endorsements from both Org1 and Org2 peers, the test-network simulates that multi-party endorsement policy. A common misconception is to assume the sandbox perfectly matches production performance or operational concerns; it does not. Instead, it captures the architectural behaviors you need to validate chaincode logic, endorsement policies, and CLI workflows. Use it to check functionally correct behavior, then move to multi-host or cloud staging when you need performance and resilience testing. The sandbox lowers the barrier to iterative development and makes debugging endorsement and channel issues tractable on a single machine. What the test-network provides means use the test-network to validate endorsement policies, channel configuration, and chaincode logic before moving to multi-host staging.. In practical terms, components, roles, and why this sandbox maps to production concepts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Best practices for a clean development environment
screens.narratorSegment: Maintaining a clean and efficient Fabric development environment saves time and reduces surprises. First, persist the PATH update to your shell profile so fabric-samples/bin is always available and you do not accidentally use system-installed or mismatched CLI versions. Second, pin or document Fabric versions used in a lab (for example the argument used to the install script) so your team reproduces identical environments. Third, always run./network. sh down after work and inspect docker ps -a to confirm no Fabric containers remain. Fourth, avoid running unrelated services on the same ports Fabric uses by convention; reserve or reconfigure host services if needed. Fifth, when switching between projects that use different Fabric releases, consider using separate workspaces or container-cleanup steps to avoid cross-contamination. A common mistake is leaving images or containers and then complaining about unexpected behavior; routine cleanup avoids that. Finally, keep a short checklist of verification commands you run before starting the network: docker --version, docker compose version, go or node versions, peer version after PATH update. These small habits ensure a predictable, repeatable development cycle and let you focus on chaincode logic instead of environment troubleshooting.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will set up a reliable Hyperledger Fabric development environment so you can run a local sandbox network and deploy sample chaincode. We will focus on the concrete tools you need — Docker and Docker Compose to host Fabric components as containers, a supported runtime for chaincode such as Go or Node. js, and classic utilities like curl and Git. You will see how to download the official fabric-samples and Fabric binaries using the provided install script, add the binaries to your PATH for convenience, and use the test-network scripts to bring up, use, and tear down a two-organization sandbox. Along the way I’ll show common pitfalls: Docker not running, permission issues, port conflicts, and environment variables that must be set when you invoke peer commands. By the end you’ll be able to run the network, create a channel, deploy the asset-transfer-basic chaincode, perform a read and a write operation, and then cleanly shut the network down. This foundation matters because a correct local environment saves hours of debugging and ensures reproducible hands-on experiments. Ready to begin with the prerequisites and the download step?

By the end of these screens you will be able to set up, run, and manage a local Hyperledger Fabric test network and perform basic chaincode interactions. First, you will identify and install required software: Docker and Docker Compose to run Fabric components as containers, a chaincode runtime such as Go or Node. js, plus curl and Git for downloads and repository management. Second, you will download the fabric-samples and Fabric binaries using the official install script, understand the directory layout created, and add the binaries directory to your PATH so the Fabric CLI tools are available anywhere. Third, you will bring up the provided test-network using the network. sh script, create a channel, and deploy a sample chaincode. Finally, you will invoke read and write operations against the chaincode and safely tear down the network. Each of these skills removes a common blocker when starting Fabric development and ensures your experiments are repeatable. We will also practice verifying installations and common quick checks that prevent the most frequent errors.

This second objectives screen focuses on the hands-on commands and environment hygiene that keep your Fabric experiments repeatable. You will practice adding the fabric-samples bin directory to your PATH so commands like peer and orderer are immediately available from your shell. You will also learn to set key environment variables used by the peer CLI to target an organization and peer, such as CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, which let you run queries and invoke transactions as a specific admin. Another objective is clean teardown: using network. sh down and, when necessary, Docker cleanup commands so stray containers and images do not cause port conflicts. Finally, you will follow best practices for version compatibility and verification so Docker images, Fabric binaries, and chaincode runtimes match. These skills prevent many common errors and speed up development iterations when building and testing chaincode.

A correct prerequisites set is the simplest, most effective risk reducer when working with Hyperledger Fabric. The core idea is straightforward: Fabric runs its components — peers, orderers, CAs, and chaincode packaging — inside Docker containers. That makes Docker and Docker Compose essential. If Docker is not running, network startup will fail immediately. For chaincode you need a supported runtime: Go or Node. js are common choices in examples; choose the runtime you intend to develop in and install the correct major version. Curl and Git are utility tools: curl fetches the install script and binaries, while Git clones the fabric-samples repository for examples and scripts. A concrete example: if Docker Desktop is stopped, running./network. sh up will produce container creation errors. A common misconception is that Fabric tools alone are sufficient — they are not; without Docker the Fabric binaries cannot start peers or orderers. Another common trap is mismatched versions: Docker engine and Compose must meet minimums, and chaincode runtime versions must match your development examples. Takeaway: verify docker --version and docker compose version, confirm go version or node -v, and ensure curl and git respond. This verification step saves multiple hours of debugging downstream.

Downloading the fabric-samples and the matching Fabric binaries is a single scripted operation that both fetches tools and aligns versions. The canonical command provided uses curl to download and run the install script with specific flags to choose a Fabric release and request Docker images and binaries. In practice you run the curl command exactly as given to create a fabric-samples directory and populate a bin folder with tools such as peer, orderer, and configtxgen. After the script completes, it is good practice to add the bin path to your shell PATH so you can run Fabric commands from any directory. A concrete example: run the curl command with the specified version label to download release 2.5.8 and include -d and -b to fetch images and binaries. A common misconception is that manually pulling Docker images is necessary; the install script handles images if invoked with the download flag. Step-by-step: run the curl line, inspect fabric-samples/bin, then export PATH=$PATH:$PWD/fabric-samples/bin and persist that line in. bashrc or. zshrc. Confirm by running peer version. This process ensures the CLI tools you need are available and version-consistent.

Bringing up the test-network is the first full end-to-end run you will perform. The network. sh script in fabric-samples/test-network orchestrates Docker container creation for two organizations, each with a peer, and a Raft ordering service. To begin, cd into fabric-samples/test-network and run./network. sh up. The script pulls or reuses Docker images, starts containers, and prepares cryptographic materials and configuration required for the network. You will see log output from containers as they initialize; this output is useful for diagnosing startup issues such as missing images or TLS certificate problems. After up completes, create a channel and deploy chaincode using the separate network. sh commands. A practical example: after./network. sh up completes, run./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel to create a channel and then./network. sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go to deploy the Go chaincode. Common mistake: running up while Docker is not started or when ports like 7051 and 7050 are already occupied by other services. Always verify Docker is running and ports are free. The network up command gives you a reproducible local Fabric environment for development and testing.

Once the network is up, the next concrete steps are creating a channel and deploying chaincode. Channels create a private ledger between organizations; in the test-network you will create mychannel to be shared by Org1 and Org2. Use./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel to create the channel and generate the necessary configuration. After the channel exists, deploy sample chaincode with./network. sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go. This deploy command packages the chaincode, installs it on peers, and commits it to the channel. A concrete example: when you run deployCC for the basic chaincode, the script compiles the Go chaincode, installs the package on both peers, approves the definition, and commits it to the channel. A frequent misunderstanding is to expect chaincode files already to be active after up; creating a channel and deploying chaincode are separate steps. Another pitfall is specifying an incorrect chaincode path or language; match -ccp and -ccl to the chaincode you intend to deploy. After deployment, you can set peer environment variables and run peer chaincode query and invoke commands to interact with ledger state. The channel and deployment sequence is the core flow for enabling application-level interactions with Fabric.

To interact with deployed chaincode you must instruct the peer CLI which organization and peer to act as. Fabric uses environment variables for this purpose. Important variables include CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, which names the MSP for the organization; CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, which points to the admin identity that will sign transactions; CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE, which references the TLS certificate for the peer; and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, which gives the host and port for the target peer. A concrete example for Org1 is to set CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID to Org1MSP and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS to localhost:7051, and to set CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH to the admin msp path provided in fabric-samples/test-network organizations structure. Once these variables are set in your shell, peer chaincode query and peer chaincode invoke commands will act under that identity. A common misconception is that the peer CLI auto-detects the intended organization; it does not. You must explicitly set these variables or source the scripts the test-network provides. Closing question: can you identify which environment variable controls the identity used for signing transactions? Answer: CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH. This explicit configuration model keeps CLI operations precise and auditable. Setting peer environment variables means set core_peer_* variables so the peer cli sends requests as a specific org admin to the correct peer endpoint.. In practical terms, configure the cli to operate as a specific organization and peer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interacting with deployed chaincode demonstrates a complete read-write cycle on the ledger. Once you’ve set peer environment variables for Org1, run a query to see current world state using peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'. This example returns an empty array initially. To create an asset, invoke the CreateAsset function with peer chaincode invoke and provide the function and arguments in JSON form, including the orderer address and TLS options. The invocation triggers transaction flow: endorsement by peers, ordering, and committing to the ledger. A concrete example is invoking CreateAsset with arguments for asset id, color, size, owner, and value. After invoking, query GetAllAssets again to verify the asset appears. A common misconception is treating invoke and query interchangeably; invoke performs state-changing transactions and requires an endorsement and orderer interaction, while query is read-only and does not generate a ledger transaction. Always ensure your peer environment variables are set and that you include correct TLS options and peer addresses when invoking across organizations. This read-then-write-then-read pattern is essential to validate chaincode behavior during development. Querying and invoking the sample chaincode means use query for reads and invoke for writes. verify results by querying after an invoke to confirm ledger updates.. In practical terms, use peer chaincode query and peer chaincode invoke to read and write ledger state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Troubleshooting a Fabric development environment is often about checking predictable causes. This screen gives a comparison of issues, likely causes, and remedies. First, 'Docker not running' manifests as container creation errors when running./network. sh up; remedy: start Docker Desktop or the Docker daemon and verify docker --version. Second, 'Permissions and sudo' may cause commands interacting with Docker to fail if your user is not in the docker group; remedy: either run with sudo where required or add your user to the docker group and re-login. Third, 'Port conflicts' show up when another service is bound to ports like 7050 or 7051; remedy: stop conflicting services or remove conflicting containers with docker ps -a and docker stop. Fourth, 'Incorrect environment variables' cause peer CLI commands to fail or target the wrong peer; remedy: re-export the CORE_PEER_* variables or source the test-network environment script. A common misconception is to assume Fabric itself is failing; often the root cause is Docker, permissions, ports, or PATH misconfiguration. When deeper issues persist, check container logs, re-run network. sh down, and consider pruning Docker images as a final corrective measure. The fastest path to resolution is to methodically validate each likely cause in this checklist.

Maintaining a clean and efficient Fabric development environment saves time and reduces surprises.
